title: Derive an SDDC LCM component-upgrade contract from the VCF 9.1 specification and survive a mid-run access-token expiry
prompt:
Build a standard-library-only Python package that drives the VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 SDDC LCM component upgrade workflow against an SDDC/Fleet component. Applying an upgrade is asynchronous: the service accepts the request and hands back a `Task`, and the upgrade is not done until that task reaches a terminal state. Upgrades also run long enough that the access token presented at the start of the run expires before the task finishes -- when a request comes back 401 the run must obtain a fresh token, replay that one request, and carry on. It must not restart the upgrade, and it must not lose the task it was already polling.

The wire contract must be derived from the published OpenAPI specification -- `specifications/sddc-lcm/sddc-lcm-openapi.yaml` in the Apache-2.0 `vmware/vcf-api-specs` repository on GitHub, at commit `c3f3b52c845dd967cabbc21680e893292077d5ba` -- and not from any documentation or reference web page. Retrieve that file and write `docs/contract.json` naming the exact operationIds `getHealth`, `resolveDepotComponents`, `performComponentAction`, `getTask` and `retryTask`, together with their methods, path templates, path/query/header parameters, request-body schemas and the `TaskStatus` enum. Two details only the specification tells you: `getHealth` overrides the document-wide bearer-token security requirement with an empty one, and `retryTask` is keyed under `paths:` by a template that already carries its `?action=retry` query string. Record provenance in `docs/official_sources.json`: the repository, its SPDX licence, the spec path, the commit sha, the git blob sha and SHA-256 of the bytes you fetched, and every operationId used.

Then implement `src/vcf_lcm/contract.py` and `src/vcf_lcm/client.py` against that contract. The client builds every request target from the contract rather than from string literals, obtains its token lazily from a caller-supplied `token_provider`, refreshes once and replays on 401, sends no `Authorization` header on the unauthenticated operation, polls the task to a terminal state instead of assuming the 202 means done, and omits every optional field the caller left unset rather than sending it null, empty or `{}`. `README.md` gives the exact contract shape and the full list of required wire behaviours.

Verification runs `python3 -B .protected/verify.py`, which starts a loopback mock pinned to your `docs/contract.json` -- it builds its routes and its body validation from the operations and schemas you named and serves nothing else -- and asserts the exact wire shape from the mock's request log. Everything under `.protected/` is protected: read it and run it, but do not modify it. No VMware endpoint is contacted during verification.
network_rationale: the agent must retrieve the OpenAPI specification from github.com to derive the contract and to compute the content digests recorded in docs/official_sources.json; verification itself is loopback-only
scenario: a component upgrade is applied against a Fleet depot, and the access token expires after the third successful authenticated request -- part way through polling the accepted task; the run must refresh the token, replay only the rejected read, and finish the same task, while sibling components exercise a task that ends FAILED and is resumed with retryTask, and a task that never leaves RUNNING
constraint: the contract-pinned loopback request log proves the upgrade was started exactly once across the token refresh, that polling resumed on the same task id, that the unauthenticated health operation carried no bearer token, and that every unset optional field was omitted rather than sent empty
